table.brief: Link inventory: Page title / URL (long unbreakable URLs) / Last checked / Status code

understanding.purpose: Audit a set of pages by associating each page and URL with its latest check date and HTTP status.
understanding.reading: Readers scan page titles to find an entry, then follow the row across to its URL, check date, and status; they may also scan dates and status codes down their columns for stale or problematic links.
groups: Page title and URL identify the same resource; the title supports recognition and the URL provides the exact destination.
Last checked and Status code describe the audit result; compact adjacent columns make dates and outcomes easy to compare.
keep_intact: URL characters and their order must remain exact, even if a URL wraps across lines.
Dates and status codes should remain intact where possible for quick comparison.
Individual words in page titles should remain intact.
may_wrap: Page titles can wrap at spaces without losing meaning.
URLs may wrap at valid break opportunities; their long unbreakable segments need sufficient width to avoid overflow or forced breaking.
Header labels can wrap if necessary, and shorter cells can use height already created by a longer title or URL in the same row.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Keep complete dates and the one-line date header, while reclaiming width from the status column for page titles. The URL retains r2C's width, so its longer entries may still need four lines.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Keep r0C's wider URL column while restoring room for whole dates and an intact status header. This tests whether the shorter URL wraps justify the narrower titles.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Preserve r0C's more readable title width, while giving dates and status-header words enough room. The URL remains wider than in r0A and r0B.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Give both audit headers their full one-line widths, producing a compact header and clearer column labels. Test the tradeoff against narrower titles and URLs; the URL column still has the stated 324px of text space needed for its longest unbreakable segment.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keep the complete dates and compact status column, but give 9px more to URLs than in date-first-balance. This tests whether longer destinations wrap more cleanly while preserving r2B's title width.

bad.name: r2A
bad.note: Give titles more room than r1A while retaining most of its URL width. Reclaim space from the date column, keeping enough room for intact dates, and check whether the first two URLs stay at three lines.
bad.why: Every date breaks before the day, making a key audit field harder to scan and compare.

bad.name: r2B
bad.note: Keep r1C's more readable title width while restoring 15px to the URL column. The narrower date column should still hold dates intact; this tests whether the extra URL space removes the four-line wraps.
bad.why: Every date breaks before the day, disrupting the repeated date column despite the shorter table.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Favor page-title recognition while keeping dates intact. Test whether the narrower URL column can still accommodate its longest unbreakable segment and produce acceptable row heights.
bad.why: The URL column is narrow enough to force a break inside a URL segment, making the identifier harder to read.

rationale: r3A gives page titles enough room to identify entries quickly while preserving complete dates on one line. The URL column remains dominant and avoids mid-word splits, although the longest addresses need four lines. The compact status column wraps its header but keeps the codes easy to scan.

general: Give repeated comparison values enough width to stay intact when possible.
Allocate width according to content and reading task; equal columns need not produce a balanced table.
Judge wrapping by where it occurs and how it affects scanning, not by table height alone.
specific: This audit benefits from single-line dates and a wide URL column, while three-digit status codes need little body width.
A slightly wider title column in r3A improves the long Salesforce title compared with r3B.

tradeoffs: r1B gives URLs more space but makes several titles more fragmented; r2C keeps all headers on one line at the expense of title and URL space. A designer could reasonably prefer either emphasis.
uncertain: The ranges are approximate, conservative estimates, not browser-tested thresholds. They describe small coupled adjustments around r3A, with the other columns adjusted proportionally and the total kept at or below 719 px; the endpoints should not be combined independently.

critique.good: All headers, dates and status codes remain intact. The compact audit columns are easy to scan, and URLs wrap without splitting words.
critique.problems: Several page titles are fragmented into three or four lines, making the identifying column harder to scan. The first two URLs also occupy four lines, creating tall rows.
critique.cause: The 150px title column is narrow, while the 345px URL column provides little room beyond the longest unbreakable segment. The 117px and 107px audit columns keep their headers on one line but consume space that could help the identifying columns.

critique.good: The 210px title column makes page titles noticeably easier to recognize, and the status codes remain easy to scan. URLs retain their characters without mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Every date wraps, separating the day from the rest of the date and making comparisons harder. Both audit headers wrap, and the first two URLs still take four lines.
critique.cause: The 90px date column is too narrow for a complete date, and the 74px status column is too narrow for its full header. The 345px URL column is unchanged from r0A.

critique.good: The 390px URL column reduces the longest URLs to three lines, while the 180px title column gives titles a useful balance of space. Most rows have a consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: Dates break after the year, and the status header splits within the word 'Status', making the audit columns difficult to read. The tall header also weakens the table's hierarchy.
critique.cause: The 85px date column cannot hold a full date, and the 64px status column leaves less than the 47px needed for the longest header word. The wide URL column takes space needed by both audit columns.

critique.good: The URL column accommodates the long segments without mid-word splits, and dates and status codes form compact, easy-to-scan columns. Titles and URLs remain clearly associated across each row.
critique.problems: Several titles are broken into three or four short lines, while both audit headers wrap. The second row is especially tall because its title takes four lines.
critique.cause: The 166px title column limits natural phrase groupings. The 108px date and 68px status columns are too narrow for their headers on one line.

critique.good: The generous URL column preserves readable URL segments, and the dates and codes stay intact. Row boundaries make the records easy to follow.
critique.problems: The narrower titles form a vertically fragmented left edge, yet the extra URL width does not reduce any row height compared with r1A. Both audit headers still wrap.
critique.cause: Reducing the title column to 150px sacrifices recognition space; increasing the URL column to 390px does not cross a useful wrapping threshold in these rows. The 111px and 68px audit columns still cannot hold their headers on one line.

critique.good: The wider title column makes the page names easier to recognize and lets the pricing row fit into two lines. Dates and status codes remain intact.
critique.problems: The first two URLs each expand to four lines, creating tall rows with empty space beneath their shorter titles. Both audit headers still wrap.
critique.cause: The 360px URL column is narrow enough to push the ends of those URLs onto extra lines. The 110px date and 69px status columns are too narrow for their full headers.

critique.good: The title and URL columns give each resource a clear identity, and most titles remain easy to recognize. URLs stay within three lines, with no mid-word splits. Status codes are compact and easy to scan.
critique.problems: Every date breaks before its final two digits, making the dates harder to compare. Both audit headers wrap, although the two-line status header remains legible.
critique.cause: The 102px date column leaves only 81px for text, less than the 96px needed for a complete date. The 68px status column is too narrow for its header on one line.

critique.good: The slightly wider title column gives page names comfortable space, while the URL column keeps the same three-line maximum as r2A. Status codes remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: The dates all split across two lines, interrupting comparison down the column. The extra title width produces little visible benefit over r2A, and both audit headers still wrap.
critique.cause: The 96px date column leaves only 75px for text. Moving width from the date column to the title and URL columns does not change the observed row heights.

critique.good: Dates and both audit headers fit on one line, making the audit results clear and easy to compare. Status codes have ample separation from the dates.
critique.problems: The narrow title column fragments several names, particularly the Salesforce title, and the first two URLs take four lines. The resulting tall rows leave substantial empty space in the audit columns.
critique.cause: The 150px title column and 345px URL column leave less room for the identifying information. The 107px status column gives its short codes more space than they need.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: The URL column is too narrow, breaking addresses into many fragments and making rows very tall, while dates and status codes have excessive space.

r1C.why: URLs have useful width, titles remain readable, and dates and codes stay intact. Both metadata headers wrap, and the longest title needs three lines.

ref_auto.why: The wide URL column comes at the expense of titles and dates: several titles take three or four lines, and every date breaks across lines.

r3A.why: Titles and URLs have a balanced share of space, dates remain intact, and status codes scan easily. Only the status header wraps.

r2A.why: Titles and URLs read reasonably well, but every date splits before the day, making comparison harder.

r1B.why: URLs have generous width and dates stay on one line, though the narrow title column makes several titles take three or four lines.

raw.unsure: B is a close alternative: it gives URLs slightly more room, but wraps both metadata headers and the longest title more than D.

r1C.why: Titles and dates remain readable, while the wide URL column limits wrapping. Both metadata headers wrap, and the longest URLs take four lines.

ref_equal.why: The narrow URL column breaks addresses and words at arbitrary points, producing very tall rows, while the date and status columns have excessive empty space.

r1B.why: URLs have useful room and dates stay intact, but the narrow title column makes several titles span three or four lines.

ref_auto.why: The wide URL column helps addresses, but every date splits across two lines and the narrow title column creates lengthy stacks.

r3A.why: Titles have enough room to read naturally, dates and the last-checked header stay on one line, and URLs retain a generous share of the width. Rows remain easy to associate across columns.

r2A.why: Titles and URLs are reasonably balanced, but every date breaks before its day, making the audit dates harder to scan and compare.

raw.unsure: A and E are close; the preferred balance depends on how much readers value slightly wider URLs versus more readable titles and the single-line date header.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
